text: Milling (ការកិនស្រូវ) turns dried paddy into edible milled rice by removing the husk and bran layers. The source distinguishes single-pass milling (កិនក្នុង១លំដាប់) — common in villages, using small hand-fed hullers (for example an Engleberg-type huller, ម៉ាស៊ីនកិនស្រូវក្នុង១លំដាប់) that hull and whiten the grain in one rough pass — from two-pass or multi-stage milling (កិនក្នុង២លំដាប់ / ច្រើនលំដាប់), which separates the process into distinct steps: cleaning the raw paddy, husking (removing the outer husk), separating husked from unhusked grain, whitening/polishing (removing the bran layer), sorting/grading by size, and packaging. Single-pass milling is cheaper and simpler but tends to produce more broken grain and a duller, less fully polished finish; multi-stage milling handles the grain more gently at each step and generally yields a higher share of whole, well-polished kernels, but needs more capital investment and larger throughput to be worthwhile. As a rough compositional guide, the source describes paddy as being made up of approximately 20% husk, 10% bran, and about 70% milled rice by weight, though the exact split varies by variety and grain condition. Getting a high milling yield of unbroken, good-quality rice depends on: starting from clean, uniform paddy that has been dried properly (moisture in the 13-14% range is the general target mentioned for grain going into storage and milling); well-maintained milling equipment correctly adjusted for the variety being processed; and careful handling after milling (sorting, packaging, and storage) to avoid reintroducing moisture, foreign material, or physical damage to the finished rice. (Note: the composition percentages and moisture target given here are illustrative averages from the source; actual milling yield and breakage depend heavily on variety, grain condition at harvest, and how well the specific mill is set up and operated.)
